# Build handover: starting M6

Written 2026-11-03, after M5 merged (`ba1f62f`). This is the resume point for the next coordinator. It covers what
to do next, how to run the work and how to decide. What earlier milestones built is in their results notes
(`docs/build/m0-results.md` to `m5-results.md`), and why things are as they are is in `docs/LOG.md`.

## 1. Where things stand

- M0 to M5 of `docs/11-build-plan.md` are on `main`. The engine runs a real ticket end to end: an agent implements in
  a sandbox, agents review, tests run in CI, and the engine merges into a parent branch. M5's live run proved this on
  the fixture repository.
- **Nothing awaits the product owner.** LOG 1 to 146 are approved. LOG 147, the simplification after M5 (eight items,
  `m5-results.md`, "Simplification after M5"), is unreviewed but its direction is approved. New judgement calls start
  at **LOG 148**.
- Tests on `main` after the simplification (`83579a1`): about 700 default, 50 integration and 19 live (providers),
  plus M5's live ticket run, which was made before the simplification. Exact counts are in `m5-results.md`.
- Only `main` exists on GitHub. No worktrees are open. The fixture repository has only `main`.

## 2. What to do next: M6, findings, validators and levels

Read M6 in `docs/11` section 4: what it builds, its done-when and its checks. Then, in order of risk:

1. **Must fix first: LOG 139.** A wait (`ci.checks`, `wait.condition`, or a merge waiting for a person) counts as an
   activity in flight. It therefore blocks the run's hand-over to a fresh Temporal run (continue-as-new) until the
   wait ends. Harmless for one ticket; it would stall an epic. The core must hand a running wait back as pending,
   keeping its records (when it began, the head it waits on), and the workflow restarts it after the hand-over.
2. **Children (M3 follow-ups 2, 3 and 10)**, which `epic_delivery` needs:
   - a child run does not receive its parent's parameters;
   - `consumes` from a parent, root or child run is not resolved;
   - a child that ends without signalling never completes its parent's `run.child` step.
3. **Re-run the done-when with real parts (LOG 146).** M5's live run used stand-ins for plan validation and the
   findings ledger, and a ticket file instead of a tracker. M6's done-when (an epic of three tickets, then a project
   over two repositories) replaces all of them.

**Follow-ups that must not be lost**

- **M4 12:** the sandbox's network is unrestricted and reaches the Temporal frontend. Fix this before any shared
  deployment.
- The rest are listed in `m5-results.md`, "Consolidated follow-ups". Pick up any that M6 touches.

Still deferred: `docs/11` open question 4 (the team deployment's object store and container platform). The effective
policy view (`docs/09` section 2.3) still needs a milestone.

## 3. How to run a milestone

This is how M5 ran. It worked, and each review stage caught real defects.

1. **Interfaces first.** One worker writes the shared interfaces, in-memory fakes and abstract contract tests on a
   milestone branch (`m6`). The coordinator reviews before anyone builds on them. Those files are then frozen: adding
   a test is fine, but changing a signature needs the coordinator.
2. **Parallel builders.** Two or three builders, each on its own branch from the milestone branch and owning
   separate files, open pull requests into the milestone branch. Give each one:
   - **its own LOG number range**, so entries never collide;
   - **its own Temporal dev server port** (M5 used 8133 to 8933);
   - **its own section** in the results note.
3. **Independent review of every pull request.** The reviewer gets the code and the design, not the builder's
   report. It must break the code itself to show that the tests catch it. In M5 every first review came back
   "changes-required", and the catches were real: a forgeable "already merged" check, forged or zero-test evidence
   counted as a pass, and CI running agent-edited workflows with the repository's secrets. Builders fix; the reviewer
   re-checks; the coordinator merges once CI is green.
4. **Integration** on the milestone branch: cross-piece tests, the live done-when run, the results note, then one
   pull request into `main`. Its own commits get a short independent review too.
5. **Merge commits only.** Delete merged branches locally and on GitHub. Clean up worktrees.

**Working with worker chats**

- Brief each worker completely: it starts with none of the coordinator's context. Each brief names:
  - the worktree and branch;
  - what siblings own;
  - the docs to read;
  - hard limits: no merges, no Slack, never print secrets;
  - the report file to write in the coordinator's session folder, with fixed headings.
- Read reports from that file. A chat transcript shows only the first 2,000 characters of each turn.
- Review diffs as they land, and decide workers' open questions quickly. Keep decisions to one message per worker.
  Queue a message when the worker is idle; steer only to change what it is doing now.
- **Worker pitfalls:**
  - This machine sets `safe.bareRepository=explicit` globally. Tests that use a bare repository need
    `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=safe.bareRepository GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=all` in the test environment only.
  - Load: one worker stressing the CPU to reproduce a flake (load average about 130) slowed every other worker's
    timing tests. Keep stress bounded.
  - A file-watching wait script must match every report file name. macOS `ls` has no `--time-style`; use
    `stat -f`.

**Reaching the product owner.** Post to the Slack channel set in `~/.ff/config.json` (`notifications.slack`) as the
Feature Factory bot. Its token is the Keychain item `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`. The bot cannot read the channel, so read
replies with the Slack MCP (`slack_read_channel`). Post at milestone transitions and for decisions only.

## 4. How to decide

The coordinator decides minor questions and records them. Only major ones go to the product owner.

- **Follow `CONTRIBUTING.md`, "Development and decision guidelines":** simple designs, repeated patterns,
  general solutions over special cases, pluggability, and challenging the design where it adds complexity a
  simpler shape would avoid. Examples from M5:
  - `test.integration` became `test.run` with a tag;
  - four runtime settings became internal constants;
  - the code host got no merge method.
- **Keep the floors, pragmatically** (`CONTRIBUTING.md`, same section). Close major loopholes and likely agent
  cheats; leave unlikely edge cases to requirements testing. M5 example of a major one: a rare duplicate CI run was
  preferred over an agent-edited workflow running with repository secrets. Independent reviewers tend to find many
  small "an agent could…" cases; triage them by likelihood and harm rather than fixing all of them.
- **A safety rule must not depend on a file the governed party can edit.** M5 applied this twice:
  - test commands come from the parent branch's manifest (LOG 138);
  - CI runs the default branch's workflow (LOG 112).
- **Evidence comes only from engine actions** (floor F7), checked against exactly the revision that is merged.
- **Verify, do not assert** (`CONTRIBUTING.md`). Every check has a control that makes it fail. Confirm workers'
  decisive claims yourself, for example a merge commit on GitHub.
- **Find the cause before relaxing a check.** The SP1 flake was the test scenario failing to produce what it
  checked; no check was relaxed.
- **What counts as major:**
  - changing a floor;
  - narrowing approved design text in a way users will notice;
  - spending or permission beyond what is approved;
  - changing the product owner's own settings or repositories.
  Everything else: decide, record a LOG entry, and list it for review at the milestone's end with a one-line
  recommendation each.
- **Log the product owner's answers where they apply.** Approved LOG text is never edited before approval. Fold
  approved "Pending review" notes into the owning document (one fact, one place).

## 5. Access and environment

| Need | How |
|---|---|
| GitHub API | `GH_TOKEN="$SPARKKZ_NZ_GITHUB_TOKEN" gh ...`. The token belongs to `sparkkz-makes`, an admin on both repositories. The default `gh` login is a Xero Enterprise Managed User account and can't write here |
| Git push | SSH through the `origin` remote, host alias `github.com-sparkkz-nz`. The same alias reaches the fixture |
| Model, for live runs | `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, held only by the model proxy. Use model `haiku` |
| GitHub App, for live runs | Key and settings in `~/keys/` (`feature-flow-github-app.pem`, `feature-flow-secrets.json`), passed as `FF_SECRETS_FILE`. Never print or commit either |
| Fixture | `ai-feature-flow/feature-flow-example`, public. Live runs there are approved and must leave no references behind. Its `main` is protected by the ruleset `protect-main` (a pull request with 0 approvals, no bypass), so the engine never merges into it |
| A live ticket run | `m5-results.md`, "The live run (M5's done-when): how to" |
| Live tests | The `Live` category, outside pull request CI. Run them to prove a done-when or a security property |
| Docker | Docker Desktop. Start it after a reboot (`open -a Docker`) |
| Temporal | `~/.temporalio/bin/temporal server start-dev --port <port> --headless`, with `FF_TEMPORAL_ADDRESS`. One port per worker |
| Merging | The coordinator may merge to `main` once CI is green and an independent review has signed off (product owner, 2026-11-03) |
